doc.title: Byron Stripling interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 25, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Questioning relevance as a jazz artist
summary: He feels a loss of relevance rather than identity, comparing Coltrane views to K-Pop and noting his wife's urging to go play.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Do you feel like in addition to the loss of income do you feel sort of like a loss of identity?

Not really. Maybe to answer the same question, loss of relevance, because musicians and artists always question their relevance, especially as a jazz musician, when you realize that jazz is the lowest selling music. You know rap is number one. My kids just showed me tonight have you heard of this group K-Pop?

It’s an all-Asian young kids and stuff, and you know, I look at John Coltrane’s “A Love Supreme” on YouTube ‘cause sometimes I’ll just put stuff on YouTube as I’m cooking or something, I’ll put on “A Love Supreme.” And maybe it’ll have 50,000 views. And I see five kids dancing around going [scats] and you know they’ve got a billion — and I’ve never seen that on a YouTube. So I know that the music I play is amazing, it’s important to me, but you start to question your relevance as, you know, hey, you know, I’ve got some videos on YouTube too you know. I don’t need a billion, but can I get a couple likes? So you start to question that. It’s part of being an artist. And every artist goes through it. Judy Garland was never happy unless she was onstage. And I have that too. My wife has indicated it, that sometimes — and this has been a difficult time — my wife will sometimes say if I have like three or four days where I don’t work she’ll like, “You need to go out and just play somewhere. Just get out of the house because you’re bugging me.” Because she knows that I get nourished by playing music. And she can’t even tell me that now, right?
